item.title: Topological Compression of Prediction Market Belief States for Event Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2610.25756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological Data Analysis (TDA) and Persistent Homology (PH) have been utilized in numerous fields$-$from protein modeling to financial analysis$-$to understand the underlying structure of data. In this paper, we incorporate TDA and PH into forecasting models over a prediction market universe to determine whether the belief state of such markets forms an underlying structure whose shape can provide predictive insight. We conclude that single-parameter PH is able to improve predictive ability and calibrated accuracy of linear forecasting models, while two-parameter multipersistence produces similar benefits for nonlinear models.
item.dc:creator: Aadit Jerfy

item.title: Probabilistic Limit Order Book Forecasting with Conditional Diffusion Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.25495v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modeling limit order book (LOB) dynamics is central to market forecasting and execution-strategy evaluation. While diffusion models achieve strong empirical performance, existing LOB snapshot models typically lack a learned recurrent encoder and formal statistical guarantees. We introduce LOBGrad, a conditional DDPM framework for probabilistic LOB forecasting that combines an autoregressive RNN encoder with a diffusion-based generator. In particular, we establish an excess-risk oracle inequality for the one-step DDPM noise-prediction objective under exponential mixing and regularity assumptions. We further show that, under contractive dynamics, the dependence on the conditioning-window length can be reduced to a dependence on the latent-state dimension. Experiments on BTC/USDT, GOOGL, and META show that LOBGrad improves on its encoder-free diffusion ablation across all reported queue metrics and obtains competitive results against other baselines. It also reproduces the key stylized facts of LOB microstructure, and yields reasonably calibrated queue-based predictive intervals. A stylized downstream task illustrates the potential value of the generated forecasts.
item.dc:creator: Junyu Chen, Franklin Liu, Moshu Xu, Lijian Yang

item.title: The Control Layer Behind Rule-Following Agents Trading Across Market Conditions
item.description: arXiv:2610.26324v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Trading discipline often fails people. Our study tested whether four AI trading agents followed their strategies and risk rules. Offering traders the evidence and an agent evaluation toolkit to separate luck from following the rules, before giving agents meaningful autonomy or capital. Our study analysed 2,627 closed positions from 12 February to 27 August 2026 across the same asset universe and execution conditions. Most positions were simulated against live prices with a 0.09% round-trip fee; 18% involved real Hyperliquid orders. Each position declared a strategy, stop and target, with a limit of five open positions per agent. The fleet finished net positive after fees. Rule adherence was high across all four agents, including the unprofitable one. Profitability tracked how often agents won relative to their break-even win rates. Institutional-style controls ran by default and contained losses through a 29% market drawdown and recovery, with documented exceptions. The discipline held for all four agents. Agents kept 97.5% of gross loss within declared stops, and typical losses closed at declared levels. Declared risk remained stable after losses and broadly stable across calm and volatile months. Twenty-three of 24 runs respected the position limit; logs identify the exception's size and duration. The same live data produced different results across assigned strategies. The trade-log tests can be rerun from the published trade snapshot; regime tests also require the published Bitcoin prices and regime labels. Section 3.5 specifies the stop-breach tolerance. These trade-level results are not account-level returns or proof of a lasting edge. Our study provides an evaluation toolkit to help traders distinguish rule-following from luck before committing capital. For anyone considering allocating capital to agents to trade, discipline should be the entry test, not the only test.
item.dc:creator: Saad Naja, Nasser Odtallah, Jake Van-Praag, Sarah May

item.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Market Making on Prediction-Market Order Books
item.description: arXiv:2610.26789v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A market maker provides liquidity by quoting prices to buy and sell an asset, earning the spread while managing inventory risk. We study market makers trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning on prediction markets, specifically Polymarket, whose thin order books pose distinct challenges. Three challenges underpin this research: adverse selection may cause a policy trained on real data to stop quoting; the consequences of a quote can arrive many steps after the action; and prediction-market L2 data does not identify individual orders needed for simulation. We address these challenges by reconstructing order-level LOBSTER-format data from Polymarket and training agents in JaxMARL-HFT on 417 real markets. We enrich the baseline market maker's observation space with the book and recent flow, redesign its actions and inventory controls, and propose a cooperative multi-agent decomposition into a quoter and a risk manager trained using recurrent Independent Proximal Policy Optimisation (IPPO) with RNN policies. We investigate reward shaping, particularly reward blending and post-fill markout, to mitigate credit-assignment difficulties between the agents. Our redesigned single-agent market maker quotes more frequently and incurs smaller held-out losses than the retrained JaxMARL-HFT baseline, although the contributions of jointly changed observations, actions and risk constraints are not separately identified. Decomposition alone performs poorly; careful reward design substantially improves the desk relative to the unshaped split and yields our best result. Models are evaluated on realised end-of-episode portfolio value on held-out markets. None establishes positive average portfolio value in periodic held-out evaluation, and each configuration was trained with one seed. The environment, data and protocol lay a foundation for makers that quote many linked markets at once.
item.dc:creator: Skander Lejmi

item.title: Combinatorial Arbitrage in Prediction Markets
item.description: arXiv:2610.23517v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a framework to identify and quantify arbitrage across logically related prediction-market contracts. We prove that prices outside the convex hull of admissible payoff vectors admit arbitrage and identify optimal arbitrage portfolios through integer programming. Using venue metadata and semantic analysis of resolution criteria, we recover 1.9 million logical relations and compile them into constraint systems covering more than 255,000 contracts. We replay full-depth Polymarket order books to simulate an arbitrageur executing these portfolios against resting orders. Among settled portfolios, an ideal arbitrageur that takes the full displayed depth of every opportunity and reuses its capital at resolution earns a risk-free return of 3.5% a week after spreads and fees. We find that arbitrage opportunities persist longer and attract less observed participation where relation discovery and execution are more costly.
item.dc:creator: Hongjian Shi, Daojing Zhai

item.title: Same Book, Different Fills: Partial Identification of FIFO Execution from Aggregate Order Books
item.description: arXiv:2609.13597v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Price-level limit order book (L2) data reveal aggregate liquidity but not the ordered queue required by price--time priority. Passive-execution backtests can therefore depend on an unobserved cancellation-allocation rule even when observed prices, quantities, and trades are held fixed. We frame recovery of market-by-order histories from aggregate snapshots as a conditional partial identification problem: multiple histories can reproduce the same aggregate path. Holding that path, reconciled market removals, latent order partitions, and additions fixed, our path-preserving compiler varies only cancellation allocation among front, quantity-weighted-random, and back rules. Within this compiler class, we establish front--back fill ordering for a virtual tagged order during one touch-price spell. We study seven months of synchronized 2025 Tokyo Stock Exchange data for two instruments with different trading activity: RIC 1301.T and RIC 7911.T. Ten-level L2 snapshots provide book states, while L1 trades permit inference of market removals and resting side through reconciliation. Each instrument contributes 1,080 matched five-minute episodes over the same 18 held-out trading days. The aggressive benchmark is invariant across FIFO realizations, but passive execution is sensitive to the cancellation rule. For 1301.T, front rather than back cancellation raises preterminal completion by 8.01 percentage points and reduces implementation shortfall by 1.010 bps. For 7911.T, the corresponding differences are 7.39 percentage points and 0.384 bps. Thus, observationally equivalent aggregate-book paths can imply economically different passive-execution outcomes. Execution policies evaluated from aggregate data should be accompanied by FIFO sensitivity analysis rather than reported as single-point estimates based on an unobservable queue assumption.
item.dc:creator: Riya Danait, Yuliana Zamora, Ioana Boier
